site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Water Toward the Punjab Fields
stories.source: Janamsakhi tradition; M. A. Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. I (1909, public domain)
body: At Haridwar, where pilgrims gathered by the Ganges, Guru Nanak watched devotees scoop water and toss it eastward as offerings for their ancestors. Then he began, quietly and calmly, to throw water westward, into the current and beyond.

The pilgrims stared and asked him what he was doing. He said, with a small smile, that he was watering his fields back in Punjab. When they laughed and said such water could never travel that far, Nanak asked, gently, how then their own water could possibly reach another world.

The laughter faded into thoughtful silence as his question landed. Nanak had not mocked their remembrance; he had invited them to think about why they did what they did. The river kept flowing, and the pilgrims went away considering, warmed by his patient humor and kind teaching.

stories.title: Mice and Elephants Remember Kindness
stories.source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: Through an abandoned village, a great herd of elephants passed on their ancient way, and many mice who lived there were crushed beneath their heavy feet. The mouse king came before the elephant king and gently asked him to lead his herd by another route, for the smallest lives were in danger. The elephant king, moved by such respectful speech, agreed at once.

Soon after, hunters trapped the elephants in thick rope nets, and the great beasts could not break free. The elephant king remembered the mice and called for help through the long grass. Thousands of grateful mice came scurrying across the dust, their tiny teeth working through the fibers until every rope fell away and the elephants stood free once more.

From that day on, the two communities lived as neighbors and friends, sharing the fields and pathways together. The mighty elephants learned never to overlook the aid of small, kind-hearted friends, and the mice knew that even the gentlest voice, spoken with respect, can shape the path of the powerful.

stories.title: Three Fishes of the Quiet Pond
stories.source: More Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1922), Project Gutenberg
body: In a sunlit pond, three fishes swam together, each with a different way of facing the world. One liked to plan ahead, another trusted his quick thinking, and the third preferred to wait and see. When fishermen's voices drifted across the water, the careful fish did not hesitate. He slipped through a hidden channel into a safer pond, grateful for the foresight he had always practiced.

The second fish lingered until the nets splashed near, but his mind stayed calm. He floated on his side, perfectly still, as if life had already left him. The fishermen, fooled by his clever stillness, tossed him back into the water, and with a flick of his tail he vanished into the deep. The third fish, who had waited too long for a miracle, was not so lucky.

Yet the pond still held hope, for two of the three had found their way to freedom. Their survival whispered a gentle truth carried through these old Jataka tales: danger can be met with preparation, or with a steady heart at the very last moment. The water settled, the channel glowed, and life went on.

stories.title: The Road-Builders of Magha
stories.source: Kulavaka Jataka, The Jataka, vol. I, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
body: In a quiet Indian village, Magha, the Bodhisatta, gathered thirty-three friends and made a gentle promise: that every day would hold some act of giving. Together they cleared the dusty roads, built rest houses for weary travelers, and dug cool ponds beneath the open sky. Their kindness became the heartbeat of the countryside, and strangers began to speak of it with warm gratitude.

But a jealous village headman whispered false accusations to the king, and elephants were sent to trample the friends. Yet the great beasts would not harm them, lowering their heads in refusal until the amazed king summoned Magha before him. When he heard of their road-building and shelter-making, the king's anger melted into admiration, and he set them free and pledged his support to their work.

When their lives gently ended, Magha was reborn as Sakka, lord of the Thirty-three Gods, and his thirty-three friends rose with him into that shining heaven. The old roads and ponds they had left behind continued to bless travelers, and the story closes as it began: with generosity multiplied, honored, and never forgotten.

stories.title: The True Bargain of Young Nanak
stories.source: Janamsakhi tradition; M. A. Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. I (1909, public domain)
body: When Nanak was still a boy, his father pressed coins into his hands and sent him down the road to buy something that would bring profit home. The path stretched between village and marketplace, warm with dust and the chatter of travelers.

Along the way he met sadhus whose robes were thin and whose stomachs were empty. Without hesitating, he spent every coin on simple food and watched the hungry holy men eat. Their faces softened, and a quiet joy rose in his own heart.

When his father asked what goods he had brought back, young Nanak answered gently that he had made a true bargain, because feeding the hungry had turned small money into lasting goodness, and in that moment wealth was named differently in their home.
